newsitem.title: UK: Britain says no early prospect of IRA truce.
newsitem.headline: Britain says no early prospect of IRA truce.

text.p: British Defence Secretary Michael Portillo ruled out an early IRA truce on Tuesday and said security had been tightened across Northern Ireland against a threat of further guerrilla attacks.

"I am afraid there is no sign of any IRA ceasefire," Portillo said in Lisburn, south of Belfast, at British Army headquarters which the Irish Republican Army (IRA) bombed last month, killing a soldier and wounding 30 soldiers and civilians.
Portillo said security forces were on the front line of a campaign that the extremists re-started last February after a 17 month lull in their 27 year battle to end British rule.

Security chiefs in London and Belfast warned recently that the IRA might strike at any moment despite intensive political efforts to get the group to declare a truce that would give a seat in peace talks to its Sinn Fein political arm.
Britain and Ireland say that Sinn Fein will not be admitted to five-month-old multi-party discussions in Belfast until the IRA declares an end to its war to unite the partitioned island.
"It seems clear that the IRA has the security forces in their targets. We therefore have to be extremely alert," Portillo told reporters.
The IRA's ability to breach security at the base and detonate two big car bombs had been a cause of concern, he said.

"In the days since that bombing, measures have been taken across the province...Everything possible to improve security has been done. We have to remain alert however to what is a very determined and very violent foe."

Portillo, making what was described as a "routine visit" to troops stationed in Lisburn and other areas of the province, said current political talks held the key to progress towards peace and would continue whether or not Sinn Fein took part.
"I don't at the moment see any prospect of a ceasefire but even without a ceasefire, the political process will continue for all those parties who accept unreservedly the democratic process."

A British newspaper reported last weekend the IRA leadership had decided on a strategy of bombings, allied to a temporary Christmas truce and an announcement on terms for a full ceasefire, in the hope of wringing concessions from Britain.
Britain, which wants the guerrillas eventually to yield up stores of hidden armaments, says the IRA must prove any future cessation is not simply a tactical respite.
"If there were a ceasefire...it would have to be unambiguous. It would have to be demonstrated by deeds as well as by words," Portillo said.
